item.title: Traffic Control Devices Manual: Selected Practitioners Reported Never or Rarely Deviating from DOT Standards
item.description:
What GAO Found
Traffic control devices consist of signs, signals, and pavement markings that communicate messages, such as warnings and guidance, to roadway users. Uniformity in these devices promotes traffic safety and efficiency across the country by reducing confusion for road users. The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) issues the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices for Streets and Highways (the “Manual”), to establish uniform national criteria for implementing these traffic control devices.
Almost all traffic engineers and other practitioners GAO interviewed from across the country said they view the Manual as the authoritative source of standards and guidance for traffic control devices. While FHWA allows for deviations from the Manual under certain conditions, including to protect vulnerable road users, almost all practitioners said they have never or rarely done so. Many practitioners told GAO that deviations risk detracting from uniformity. Several reported having deviated occasionally to save on costs or to address local issues affecting efficiency or safety. Many traffic engineers were reluctant to deviate from the Manual’s requirements due to the possibility of facing a lawsuit if a crash were to occur at the site where the deviation occurred.
FHWA revises and updates the Manual and considers feedback from practitioners in doing so. This feedback includes change requests and successful experiments that tested new devices or applications. See examples of new devices included in the most recent edition of the Manual in the figure below.
Examples of Traffic Control Devices to Enhance Safety for Vulnerable Road Users from the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition (2023)
FHWA maintains a public online database tracking requests for experiments, interpretations, and changes to the Manual. But, the database provides few details on experiments or change requests. FHWA told GAO it has this information and provides it to practitioners upon request. However, this option is not clearly stated on FHWA’s website, and many practitioners are unaware of it. By more clearly communicating this option on its website, FHWA would provide practitioners with greater access to information about experiments on traffic control devices. Such information could help practitioners develop and prepare their own requests and test devices and applications on the roads they operate, thus promoting the Manual’s objectives of safety and efficiency.
Why GAO Did This Study
Engineers use the Manual to deploy traffic control devices uniformly across the U.S. Under certain limited conditions, localities may deviate from the Manual and deploy traffic control devices differently than it requires or recommends. Safety organizations have expressed concerns that engineers may be unwilling to deviate even when doing so might make roadways safer for vulnerable road users like pedestrians and cyclists.
GAO was asked to review issues related to how practitioners deviate from the Manual to protect vulnerable road users. This report examines: (1) how selected practitioners use the Manual and under what circumstances they deviate from it and (2) how FHWA updates the Manual and communicates with stakeholders on potential new uses of traffic control devices.
GAO reviewed the Manual, FHWA’s Official Rulings Database and other sections of its website, as well as relevant regulations and statutes. GAO interviewed agency officials; practitioners from a non-generalizable sample of 26 city, county, and state jurisdictions nationwide; as well as traffic engineers and other practitioners from five selected professional membership organizations.
